nodes.question: Why doesn't every describable collection qualify as a legitimate set?
nodes.why: The permission to define a predicate is not permission to collect all satisfying objects into a set.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: Set constructions are constrained by foundational axioms. Relations, products, functions and equivalence classes create new objects; unrestricted self-referential comprehension leads to contradiction.

nodes.question: Can existence be proven without producing a computable example?
nodes.why: An existential proof by choice need not be an algorithm with a feasible runtime.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: Choice, well-ordering, Zorn maximality and transfinite recursion support existential arguments. Halmos explicitly distinguishes these foundations; functional-analysis extension theorems use related ideas.

nodes.question: When are two differently described mathematical objects really the same?
nodes.why: A continuous bijection need not have a continuous inverse; shared size is not shared structure.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: Bijections preserve cardinality; linear and group isomorphisms preserve algebraic operations; homeomorphisms preserve topology. Each equality-up-to-structure has different invariants.

nodes.question: Why does changing coordinates not change the underlying linear map?
nodes.why: A matrix and its represented transformation must not be conflated; invertible basis changes preserve rank.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: Vector spaces support basis-free addition and scaling; a matrix is a representation after choosing bases. Kernel, rank and nullity constrain linear maps independently of coordinate systems.

nodes.question: When can a transformation be separated into independent modes?
nodes.why: Diagonalizability is not automatic for a general matrix, let alone an unbounded function operator.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: Eigenvectors and invariant subspaces expose stable directions. Spectral theorems need normality or self-adjointness; Jordan structure and infinite-dimensional continuous spectra expose limitations.

nodes.question: How do reversible transformations form reusable algebraic structure?
nodes.why: Quotients by arbitrary nonnormal subgroups do not inherit well-defined group multiplication.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: A group is composition with identity and inverses. Homomorphisms preserve operation; cosets/normal subgroups permit quotients, and representations turn transformations into matrices.

nodes.question: How can symmetry reduce counting and computation?
nodes.why: The counted equivalence depends on whether reflections, rotations or relabelings belong to the action.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: A group action partitions objects into orbits with stabilizers. Representation characters encode transformation behavior; equivalent configurations may be counted once rather than repeatedly.

nodes.question: Why might factorization stop being unique when the number system changes?
nodes.why: Prime elements, irreducibles and prime ideals are different notions unless additional hypotheses hold.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: Ring multiplication supports ideals, quotient rings and varying notions of primality. Quadratic integer domains can lose unique factorization of elements while ideals recover a structured replacement.

nodes.question: How can algebra prove a classical construction cannot be performed?
nodes.why: Failure to discover a radical expression is not proof of impossibility; allowed operations must be fixed.
nodes.mechanism_explanation: Field extensions and automorphism groups encode algebraic relations among roots. Artin uses degree restrictions to distinguish constructible lengths from impossible ruler-and-compass requests.
